response.reasoning: This is a discrete weather event, not a tracker defect. WO-2025-00218 states the work is cleanup after a microburst on the 14th and logs it against property claim NRS-PL-2025-0417; WO-2025-00268 and WO-2025-00349 both open with 'Storm damage'. The damage modes are varied and mechanical (bent dampers, purlins out of true, sheared couplings, pulled clamps), which is what a single wind loading event produces, not what a repeating component defect produces. All twenty tickets fall between 2025-03-15 and 2025-04-28 and the site returns to baseline afterwards. Hypothesis H3 also holds partial credit: the cluster mixes per-row tags (WO-2025-00227, WO-2025-00257) with per-zone tags whose narratives each account for many rows (WO-2025-00278 reports nine rows in one ticket, WO-2025-00387 another nine), so the twenty tickets represent materially fewer physical events. No warranty claim against the tracker OEM is supportable.
response.contradicting_evidence: Two tickets (WO-2025-00350, WO-2025-00324) describe the same torque-tube-out-of-true finding weeks apart, which could indicate an incomplete first repair rather than fresh storm damage. Worth a spot check, but it does not change the verdict.

population_at_risk.description: None. Damage is confined to one site and one event.

response.reasoning: Every affected serial is a KVP-3600 built in 2024 within a narrow week band: 2419B (week 19), 2423B (23), 2428C (28), 2432C (32), 2434C (34). No unit from any other build year appears, and the installed base shows KVP-3600 spread across build years from 2015 to 2024, so this is a cohort effect rather than a model-wide or age effect. The failure mode is consistent and physical: IGBT modules discoloured with heat-marked busbars (WO-2026-00480, WO-2026-00696, WO-2026-00702) escalating to units that shut down hard and will not restart (WO-2026-00514, WO-2026-00575, WO-2026-00595). Two units recur - KVP36-2428C-0169 in WO-2026-00522 then WO-2026-00575, and KVP36-2419B-0365 in WO-2026-00480 then WO-2026-00579 - which is progressive damage, not independent random failure. WO-2026-00522 records the unit was still on firmware revision 4.2.1. Peer models show zero tickets with this symptom, so H2 (ordinary wear) and H3 (site conditions) both fail: other models co-located at these sites are not producing thermal damage.
response.contradicting_evidence: All eight tickets fall in May and June 2026, the last two months of the data window, so the observed severity may be a late-window artifact of a defect that has been developing unobserved. This makes the cost figure a floor rather than a settled total.

response.business_headline: 74 Kelvara KVP-3600 inverters from one 2024 build window are failing thermally while still inside parts warranty - a supplier claim on damage already incurred plus a billable remediation campaign across the cohort.

response.reasoning: TECH-0231 tags 94 percent of tracker work at row level against a fleet average of 51 percent, and the habit persists across three separate sites (Sundowner Mesa, Joshua Fork, Ashvale Dry Lake) from March 2025 through June 2026, so it is a standing practice rather than an artifact of any one campaign. His per-row tickets are small and single-scope - WO-2025-00285 replaces one stow pin, WO-2025-00794 retorques one damper bolt, WO-2026-00187 the same - averaging under three hours. Peer tickets at the same sites carry zone tags and describe several rows of work each. The effect is that any count of tracker events at Mojave sites is inflated roughly threefold wherever this technician worked, which distorts site reliability comparisons and inflated candidate CAND-001. This is real and worth fixing, but it carries no direct revenue or warranty consequence.
response.contradicting_evidence: Per-row logging is arguably more accurate, not less - the fleet norm may be the deficient convention. The fix should be to standardise, not necessarily to move this technician to zone-level tagging.

population_at_risk.basis: Data quality finding; exposure is to reporting accuracy, not equipment.

response.reasoning: Same event as CAND-001, viewed through a different aggregation. Eighty-two percent of this site's tracker-structure tickets fall in the eight weeks starting 2025-03-16, two days after the microburst named in WO-2025-00218. The damage descriptions are the varied mechanical signature of wind loading on rows caught partway to stow - bent purlins (WO-2025-00223, WO-2025-00349), torque tubes out of true (WO-2025-00324, WO-2025-00350), pulled clamps and damaged stow pins. H2 requires the elevated rate to persist beyond the window and it does not. The remaining 18 percent of this site's tracker-structure tickets are spread across the other 22 months, which is the correct baseline comparison.
response.contradicting_evidence: None identified. The temporal bound is unambiguous.
response.recommended_action: No fleet action. Verify the property claim captured the full repair cost including the rows left stowed pending parts in WO-2025-00278 and WO-2025-00383.
response.business_headline: The same March 2025 wind event seen a second way - time-bounded, insured, and not a Trackline H2 defect.

response.reasoning: Nine tickets over two years describing hardened or separated grease and scored gear faces on tracker drives. The technicians characterise it themselves as expected: WO-2024-00061 and WO-2025-01170 both record grease separated and repacked with no further comment. Arrivals are steady from July 2024 to January 2026 rather than bursting, which fits end-of-grease-life on an original-vintage population, not a defect. Recorded production loss across the whole cluster is 4.5 MWh, which is immaterial. H2 would require failures well short of design life and a rate sharply worse than same-vintage peers; instead the same pattern appears independently at two other older sites, which points to vintage rather than to a bad batch here.
response.contradicting_evidence: Whether preventive lubrication was actually being performed on schedule is not visible in this cluster. If it was not, part of this cost is avoidable and the finding would move from wear to backlog.

population_at_risk.description: Not quantifiable from this data - tracker drives are not in the serial-level asset registry.

response.recommended_action: Fold into the fleet-wide slew-drive lubrication policy review triggered by the same pattern at Dry Creek Junction and Red Clay Flats rather than treating as a site issue.
response.business_headline: Routine end-of-life grease service on original-vintage tracker drives - real work, negligible production impact, no supplier exposure.

response.reasoning: Technicians state the conclusion outright. WO-2024-00012 records the rows are all about due; WO-2024-00306, WO-2025-00535 and WO-2025-00537 each describe this being the third drive in the block that quarter and explicitly call it normal wear for the vintage. Eight tickets spread evenly across two years with 4.8 MWh of recorded loss. H2 remains live at fleet level - this is the second of three independent sites showing the same symptom on the same tracker model - but at site level there is nothing to escalate.
response.contradicting_evidence: Three sites showing the same wear symptom on the same tracker model could indicate a genuine design shortfall in grease service interval rather than normal wear. That question is answerable but not from this cluster alone.
response.recommended_action: Combine with the Ashvale Dry Lake and Red Clay Flats clusters into one fleet-level review of slew-drive lubrication intervals on 2016-2019 vintage Auster trackers.
response.business_headline: Expected grease-life maintenance on older tracker drives - low value individually, worth one fleet-level interval review across the three affected sites.

response.reasoning: Taken alone this site looks like routine wear, and the narratives read that way - WO-2024-00054 calls it normal for the vintage, WO-2026-00688 notes the same thing happening on neighbouring rows. But this is the third independent site with the identical symptom on the same tracker model and vintage, and recorded production loss is zero, so the case is a maintenance-policy case rather than a reliability case. WO-2025-01195 records a technician wondering how many more are due, which is the practical question: the cost here is recurring truck rolls for work that a shortened preventive lubrication interval would absorb more cheaply. Escalation is not warranted because the financial impact is small and there is no supplier exposure.
response.contradicting_evidence: Zero recorded lost production may simply reflect that nobody estimated it on tracker tickets rather than that there was none. A stalled row does lose generation.

population_at_risk.basis: Tracker drives are not serial-registered; the registry covers central inverters only.

response.recommended_action: Commission one fleet-level review of slew-drive lubrication intervals covering the 2016-2019 Auster population across Ashvale Dry Lake, Dry Creek Junction and Red Clay Flats.
response.business_headline: A real three-site wear pattern on older Auster tracker drives worth one maintenance-interval review - not a warranty claim and not urgent.

response.reasoning: This is the same population as CAND-002 at an earlier severity stage. Every serial falls in the 2024 build window: 2419B (week 19), 2426B (26), 2427C (27), 2428C (28), 2436C (36). KVP36-2428C-0169 appears here derating in WO-2025-00908 and then appears in CAND-002 with power-stage thermal damage in WO-2026-00522 and WO-2026-00575, which is the progression made explicit on a single unit. KVP36-2419B-0361 recurs within this cluster (WO-2024-00163 then WO-2025-00688). The narratives describe afternoon-heat derating with no fault logged and nothing to reset, and technicians escalated to the OEM without resolution in WO-2025-00688, WO-2025-00908 and WO-2026-00586. H3 (fouling) fails because the same technicians report intakes and heat sinks clear. H2 (designed behaviour) fails because peer models at the same sites do not generate equivalent tickets.
response.contradicting_evidence: Derating is genuinely normal protective behaviour at high ambient, so a portion of these tickets may be correct operation reported as a fault. That would reduce the count but not the cohort pattern.

response.reasoning: Mildest presentation of the same cohort fault. Affected serials again sit in the 2024 window: 2422B (week 22), 2423B (23), 2432C (32), 2435C (35). Units recur within a season - WO-2025-00248 and WO-2026-00627 both record a second over-temperature trip on a 2422B unit that season - and technicians report the intake and heat sinks clear on inspection, which is what separates this from ordinary fouling. WO-2025-00248 records a technician speculating in writing that fan control may be ramping late, and no one escalated it. Confidence is medium rather than high because the cluster is genuinely mixed: WO-2025-01068 found filters completely blocked, a straightforward maintenance cause that belongs to H2 and not to the cohort fault.
response.contradicting_evidence: WO-2025-01068 identifies a physical cause (blocked filters) and should be excluded from the cohort. At least one member of this cluster is ordinary maintenance, so the count overstates the cohort effect.

response.reasoning: Ground faults on this model are balance-of-plant events, not inverter faults. Every narrative locates the cause outside the inverter: a home run chafed against racking in WO-2024-00002, pinched connectors in combiners in WO-2025-00524, WO-2026-00229 and WO-2026-00699. Affected serials span 2016 to 2024 builds (1629C, 1635C, 1743D, 1845D, 1922B, 2438C) with no cohort concentration. Decisively, the normalised rate is 0.082 faults per installed unit against a peer median of 0.073 - the same symptom appears on CE-4000 at 0.073, MG-3300 at 0.080 and KVP-2400 at 0.046. This is a fleet baseline phenomenon appearing here only because KVP-3600 has the largest installed base. Escalating it would be a false positive.
response.contradicting_evidence: Thirty-one tickets and 160 labour hours is real recurring cost even if it is not a defect. There may be a workmanship case at specific sites, which is a different and smaller finding than the one tested here.

population_at_risk.basis: Rate is at fleet baseline across all four inverter models.

response.reasoning: This cluster mixes two causes and should not be actioned as one. Older units have ordinary physical causes: WO-2024-00278 found a bird nest in the intake plenum of a 2016-build unit, WO-2025-00789 a seized fan on a 2019 build. Units from the 2024 window show the different and more interesting pattern - WO-2025-00920 and WO-2026-00693 both report the fan bank running, airflow low across the stack, and filters found not particularly dirty, which is the signature that belongs with the CAND-002 cohort rather than with maintenance. Because roughly half the cluster is routine work, the normalised lift of 2.16 overstates the cohort effect and the cluster as constructed is not a clean finding.
response.contradicting_evidence: Splitting this cluster by manufacture cohort was not done in aggregation, so the split above is inferred from a sample rather than measured across all 17 members.

response.reasoning: The technicians establish the commercial answer directly: WO-2025-00135 records that production was never affected and only reporting drops, and WO-2024-00288 confirms the unit was generating normally per the meter while showing offline in the portal. Recorded lost production across the cluster is 0.1 MWh against 10.6 labour hours. This is a genuine recurring nuisance on Soltera ST-250 comms modules at a humid site, and it is real enough to fix, but it converts to almost no money. H2 fails on the metered evidence.
response.contradicting_evidence: Repeated dispatches to a fault with no production consequence still consume technician capacity that has an opportunity cost not captured in the energy figure.

response.reasoning: The normalised rate here is 0.073 per installed unit against a peer median of 0.080 - this model is slightly better than its peers, and the cluster exists only because 327 units generate a lot of absolute tickets. This is the clearest illustration in the run of why raw counts mislead: 24 tickets and 113 labour hours look material until divided by installed base. Causes are again external to the inverter - a pinched connector in WO-2024-00069, a chafed home run in WO-2024-00185, no fault found in WO-2025-00084, WO-2025-01248 and WO-2026-00670.
response.business_headline: Calderon ground faults run below the fleet average once normalised by installed base - a volume artifact, not a finding.

response.reasoning: Residual cleanup from the same March 2025 wind event. The physical finding in the April tickets is a bent limit-switch bracket - mechanical deformation, not calibration drift - in WO-2025-00286, WO-2025-00344 and WO-2025-00375, and WO-2025-00286 opens with a technician noting it is the same as the others that month. Seven of nine members fall in the weeks after the event. H2 would require drift-type language and steady arrivals across the window; instead arrivals collapse after April with only WO-2025-00930 and WO-2026-00073 following later, both of which read as ordinary recalibration. H3 also contributes: eight of nine members carry per-row tags from the same technician identified in CAND-003.
response.contradicting_evidence: Two members fall well outside the event window and are genuinely routine recalibration, so the cluster is not purely event-driven. This does not change the verdict but the cluster boundary is imprecise.

population_at_risk.basis: Event-bounded and inflated by per-row logging.
